title: The Interview
summary: The chapter has two parts. Part I, from Christopher Silvester’s introduction to an anthology of interviews, traces the history of the interview and the very mixed opinions famous writers hold about it. Part II is an extract from Mukund Padmanabhan’s interview with Umberto Eco, in which the Italian scholar and novelist explains how he finds time for so much work and why his novel The Name of the Rose became a bestseller.

notes.heading: About the authors
notes.html: Christopher Silvester (born 1959) is a British journalist and editor of The Penguin Book of Interviews. Mukund Padmanabhan is an Indian journalist who interviewed Umberto Eco (1932–2016), Italian semiotician, philosopher and author of The Name of the Rose, for The Hindu.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: Part I says the interview, invented a little over 130 years ago, is now a common feature of journalism. Some regard it as an art and a source of truth; many celebrities see it as an intrusion. Writers such as V. S. Naipaul, Lewis Carroll, Rudyard Kipling, H. G. Wells and Saul Bellow expressed dislike of it. Yet it remains a powerful means of communication and gives the interviewer great influence. Part II shows Eco explaining that he uses ‘interstices’, the empty spaces in the day, to work; that he sees himself chiefly as an academic who writes novels on Sundays; and that the success of The Name of the Rose is a mystery, though its timing may have helped.

notes.heading: Part I: detailed summary
notes.html:
History and spread. The interview became a journalistic form since its birth in the nineteenth century. Today almost every literate person has read one, and thousands of celebrities have been interviewed.

Mixed opinions. Some value interviews as a source of truth and an art in practice. Most celebrities, however, consider themselves victims. Naipaul felt that people are hurt by interviews and lose part of themselves. Lewis Carroll was said to have a horror of interviewers and never agreed to be interviewed. Kipling went further, calling it immoral, a crime and an assault deserving punishment, and his wife noted in her diary that two reporters from Boston had ruined their day. H. G. Wells described it as an ordeal, though he himself interviewed Stalin. Saul Bellow compared interviews to thumbprints on the windpipe.

Value of the interview. Despite these drawbacks, the interview is a supremely serviceable medium of communication. Through it, readers get vivid impressions of contemporaries. The interviewer holds a position of unprecedented power and influence.

notes.heading: Part II: detailed summary
notes.html:
Eco’s productivity. Padmanabhan notes that Eco has written scholarly works on semiotics, literary interpretation and medieval aesthetics, as well as children’s books and novels. Eco answers that he has a secret: the universe has empty spaces, which he calls interstices, and he uses these spare moments, such as waiting for a lift, to work.

Unity of his work. Eco says he is not doing many things but one: pursuing his philosophical interests on ethics, truth and language through academic work and novels alike. He wrote his scholarly books in a narrative, story-telling style, which was unusual, and this made the transition to novels natural.

Academic first. He calls himself a university professor who writes novels on Sundays. He attends academic conferences rather than meetings of novelists and identifies with the academic community.

The Name of the Rose. The novel, a demanding detective story set in a medieval monastery that also explores theology and history, sold between 10 and 15 million copies. Eco calls its success a mystery. He believes it might not have succeeded had it come out ten years earlier or later. He also observes that journalists and publishers assume readers want only easy reading, but readers do enjoy difficult, challenging books.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• The interview as a double-edged medium: informative yet intrusive.
  • Privacy versus publicity: the celebrity’s right to privacy against the public’s curiosity.
  • Time management and discipline: Eco’s use of interstices.
  • Readers’ intelligence: serious books can find a mass audience.

notes.heading: Character sketch: Umberto Eco
notes.html: Eco comes across as witty, modest and deeply intellectual. He gives a playful answer about his ‘secret’ of empty spaces, refuses to see himself as a great novelist, and values his scholarly identity above fame. He respects readers and challenges the assumption that only light reading sells. His views reveal a disciplined mind that unites philosophy and storytelling.

notes.heading: Title justification
notes.html: The title suits both parts: Part I discusses the interview as a form of communication, and Part II is itself an example of an interview. Together they show the theory and the practice of the interview.

notes.heading: Message and values
notes.html: Interviews must be conducted with respect for the subject’s dignity. Productive people make use of small moments, and genuine intellectual work can reach a wide audience when it is presented engagingly.

questions.q:
Read the situation and answer: Silvester notes that while some see the interview as an art and a source of truth, most celebrities feel they are its victims.
(a) Name any two writers who disliked being interviewed. (1)
(b) Why do celebrities feel like victims? (1)
(c) What positive view of the interview is mentioned? (1)
(d) Find a word meaning ‘a person harmed by something’. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) V. S. Naipaul and Rudyard Kipling (also Lewis Carroll, H. G. Wells, Saul Bellow).

(b) Interviews invade their privacy and may misrepresent them.

(c) It is seen as an art and a source of truth, a valuable medium of communication.

(d) Victim.

questions.q: What are some of the positive views on interviews?
questions.answerHtml: Interviews are considered a supremely serviceable medium of communication. Some regard them as an art and a source of truth. Through them readers get vivid impressions of famous contemporaries, and the interviewer enjoys great power and influence over public opinion.

questions.q: Why do most celebrity writers despise being interviewed?
questions.answerHtml: They feel interviews intrude upon their privacy and can distort their views. Naipaul felt people lose a part of themselves, Kipling considered it an assault, and Saul Bellow found it suffocating, like thumbprints on the windpipe. Hence they feel victimised.

questions.q: What is Eco’s ‘secret’ of doing so many things?
questions.answerHtml: Eco says he uses the ‘interstices’, the empty spaces of time that everyone has in a day. For example, while waiting for a lift or a guest, he writes or thinks. By using these small gaps, he manages academic work, novels and children’s books.

questions.q: Discuss the varied opinions on interviews expressed in Part I of the chapter. Which do you agree with and why? (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Part I presents sharply divided opinions about interviews. On the positive side, some see the interview as an art and a source of truth. It is a highly useful medium of communication that gives readers vivid impressions of their contemporaries and gives the interviewer unprecedented influence.

On the negative side, many celebrities feel victimised. Naipaul believed interviews wound people and take away part of their personality. Lewis Carroll had a horror of interviewers and protected his privacy. Kipling condemned the interview as immoral and criminal, while Wells called it an ordeal and Saul Bellow compared it to thumbprints on the windpipe.

I agree that interviews are valuable, since they make the thoughts of eminent people accessible to millions. However, I also believe interviewers must respect privacy and report faithfully. When conducted with sensitivity, an interview informs readers without harming the person interviewed.

questions.q: What impression of Umberto Eco do you form from the interview? (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Umberto Eco emerges as a brilliant yet modest and witty intellectual. Though he wrote on semiotics, philosophy, history and literature, as well as novels and children’s books, he does not boast. Asked how he does so much, he playfully reveals his ‘secret’ of using the interstices of the day, showing discipline and good humour.

He has clarity about his identity. He considers himself first a scholar and university professor who writes novels only on Sundays, and he prefers academic conferences to literary gatherings. He sees all his work as one unified pursuit of philosophical ideas.

Eco is also honest and thoughtful. He admits that the enormous success of The Name of the Rose is a mystery and credits timing. He respects readers’ intelligence, arguing that they enjoy difficult books. Overall, he appears scholarly, humble, disciplined and engaging.
